introduction-its-not-public-domain.core: Code being visible on GitHub doesn't mean you can use it freely. Copyright applies by default, and only the licence grants you rights, with conditions. No licence means no permission.

first_principles.problem: Developers copy code from public repos without a licence check, exposing the company to legal claims.
truths: Licences grant specific permissions with conditions.
derivation: **No licence = don't use it** (or ask the author).

analogy.title: A library book
analogy.story: You can read it, but you can't photocopy and sell it unless the publisher allows that.
analogy.breaks: This isn't legal advice. Involve counsel for real decisions.

example.title: A snippet from a repo with no LICENSE
flow: Find useful code, no LICENSE file
Ask author or find licensed alternative
example.outcome: licence checks happen before code is reused.

check.q: What rights do you have to public code with no licence?
check.a: Essentially none beyond viewing it, because copyright reserves all rights by default.

permissive-licenses-do-what-you-want.core: MIT, BSD and Apache 2.0 let you use, modify, sell and close-source the code. You mainly keep copyright and licence notices; Apache 2.0 adds an explicit patent grant and change notices.

first_principles.problem: Teams need to know which licences are safe defaults for proprietary products.
derivation: **MIT/BSD**: keep the copyright and licence text.
**Apache 2.0**: plus a NOTICE file, modification notices and a **patent grant**.

analogy.title: A gift with a small sticky note
analogy.story: 'Use it however you like, just keep this note saying who made it.'
analogy.breaks: Forgetting attribution is still a licence violation.

example.title: Shipping a product with MIT and Apache libraries

check.q: What does Apache 2.0 add over MIT?
check.a: An explicit patent licence grant (with termination on patent litigation) and NOTICE/change-notice requirements.

copyleft-licenses-share-and-share-alike.core: Copyleft licences require derivative works to be released under the same licence. GPL triggers on distribution, AGPL also on network use (SaaS), and LGPL allows dynamic linking from proprietary code.

first_principles.problem: Linking a GPL library into a distributed proprietary product can oblige you to release your source.
truths: Copyleft protects user freedom over developer freedom.
The trigger matters: distribution vs network access.
derivation: **GPL**: distribute a derivative → share source under the GPL.
**AGPL**: users interacting over a network → share source.
**LGPL**: dynamic linking OK; changes to the library itself must be shared.

analogy.title: A sourdough starter shared on condition
analogy.story: You can use the starter, but any bread starter you pass on must come with the same sharing condition.
analogy.breaks: Internal use without distribution generally doesn't trigger the GPL, but AGPL changes that for network services.

example.title: A SaaS using an AGPL database fork

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: AGPL is often banned in SaaS companies.

example.outcome: copyleft obligations are understood before adoption.

check.q: Why is AGPL especially relevant for SaaS?
check.a: It triggers source-sharing obligations when users interact with the software over a network, even without distribution.

the-license-compatibility-matrix.core: Combining code under different licences in one work is only legal if their terms can all be satisfied at once. Permissive code can flow into GPL projects, but GPL code can't flow into proprietary or some permissive-licensed works.

first_principles.problem: A project mixes Apache 2.0 and GPLv2 code, and the combination is incompatible.
truths: Each licence sets conditions on the combined work.
Conflicting conditions can't both be met.
Direction matters (permissive → copyleft is usually fine).
derivation: Check the **whole dependency tree**, transitives included.

analogy.title: Mixing chemicals
analogy.story: Some combine safely; others react. You check the compatibility chart before mixing.
analogy.breaks: The matrix is a simplification. Edge cases need legal review.

example.title: An audit finds a GPLv2 transitive dependency
flow: SCA flags GPLv2 deep in tree

check.a: No, though it is compatible with GPLv3.

risk-strategy-for-enterprise.core: Enterprises make compliance a guardrail: an approved/review/banned licence policy, automated licence scanning in CI, SBOMs with licence data, attribution generation and a legal escalation path.

first_principles.problem: You can't expect every developer to be a licence lawyer, but every dependency carries legal risk.
truths: Most licences fall into clear categories.
derivation: Define tiers: **Approved** (MIT, BSD, Apache), **Review** (LGPL, MPL), **Banned** (AGPL, unlicensed).
**Scan in CI** (FOSSA, ORT, Trivy licence mode).

analogy.title: A company's approved vendor list
analogy.story: Approved vendors need no paperwork, some need sign-off, and some are blacklisted.
analogy.breaks: Licence detection tools can misidentify licences, so review edge cases.

example.title: A PR adds an AGPL dependency
flow: Dev picks MIT alternative or requests exception

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No lawyer in the loop for the 95% of clear cases.

example.outcome: licence risk is managed at scale.

check.q: What's a common banned licence in SaaS companies?
check.a: AGPL, because of its network-use source disclosure trigger.
